newsitem.title: UK: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest - Mar 25.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest - Mar 25.

text.p: REUTERS EMERGING EUROPE PRESS DIGEST FOR ADVERTISING & MEDIA
Weekly Press Digest from Central and Eastern Europe on Advertising, Marketing, the Media, the Internet, Brand-name Products and Consumer Trends
ADVERTISING & MARKETING:

-- The cost of advertising on television and radio has recently fallen in the Czech Republic. Of the three nationwide TV stations, it costs most to advertise on Nova TV at 230,000 crowns ($7,870) for a half-minute evening spot. It costs 80,000 crowns less on Ceska Televize, while a half-minutes ad before the news costs only 19,000 crowns on Prima. (Hospodarske Noviny, March 20, 1997)

-- Expend Kft will soon launch multimedia software that analyses total advertising expenditure in Hungary. The new service will compete with Mediagnozis, which accounts for 85 percent of advertising cost statistics. The Expend Kft software will provide adspend figures for the six major television and seven radio channels, 180 different newspapers as well as billboards and cinema advertising. (Vilaggazdasag, March 20, 1997)
-- The largest alcohol advertiser in the Czech Republic last year was Johnnie Walker, which spent nearly 30 million crowns on advertising. (Strategie, March 12-19, 1997)
-- Bulgarias Advertising Agencies Association plans to pass a code of practice for ad agencies this year. It also decided to hold a National Advertising Forum, following its 1996 forum.
(Pari, March 19)

-- Talks between Bulgarian National Television and ad agency representatives failed to settle differences over pricing. Television pricing is expected to change after the introduction of a "currency board system" in June, which will peg the lev to the dollar or mark. (Pari, March 19)
-- Companies spent more than $35 million on market research in Poland last year, $5.0 million more than in 1995, the Polish Market Research Association said.
A seminar on Poland's market research industry will be held in Zakopane, southern Poland this month by the Krakow-based firm, Eskadra. (Gazeta Wyborcza, Market research supplement, March-April, 1997)

-- As a result of Hungary's sports law passed in July 1996, which places sports financing on a commercial footing, the money value of sports sponsorship may double, said Otto Torok, director of the Hungarian Olympic Committee (MOB). He said an agreement was also about to be signed with broadcast media to allow sports sponsors to appear on TV free of charge.
(Vilaggazdasag, March 20, 1997)

-- MARK/BBDO ad agency won the account for Heinz-PMV in the Czech Republic, which makes children's dairy products and powdered milk. Bates/Saatchi & Saatchi, Cernak Christie Landberg and DDB also pitched for the account. MARK/BBDO also won the advertising account for the magazine Tyden, after competing against Grey and Ammirati Puris Lintas. (Strategie, March 12-19, 1997)
-- Pepsi reappointed Ogilvy & Mather in Bulgaria. (Pari, March 19)
MEDIA AND THE INTERNET:

-- Central European Media Enterprises (CME) said it would increase its stake in the Czech Independent Television Corporation (CNTS) -- which controls Nova television -- by 5.2 percent to 91.2 percent of broadcasting rights and 93.2 percent of the company's assets. (Pravo, March 17, 1997)

-- The general director of the Czech TV station, Ceska Televize, Ivo Mathe, said it was common business practice for the station to have provided sound for the opposition Social Democratic Party's (CSSD) recent political convention and he dismissed criticism by the Civic Democratic Party. He said the deal did not mean the station supported the CSSD. (Pravo, March 20, 1997)
-- Agora, the publisher of Gazeta Wyborcza daily in Poland, will buy a 20 percent stake in Canal Plus Polska television from Polcom Invest, which holds a 67 percent stake in the company.
(Zycie, March 20, 1997)
-- The Polish-language version of Cosmoplitan women's magazine will be issued in May with an initial print run of 200,000 copies. It will cost 4.9 zlotys ($1.58) each, Cosmopolitan said.
(Nowa Europa, March 17, 1997)

-- Nearly 200,000 viewers of the Prague cable television networks Kodis, Dattel and Innet can now receive broadcasting from the third Czech commercial television station Galaxie, which officially began broadcasting at Christmas 1996 in the cities of Hradec Kralove and Pardubice. The Galaxie network, which aims to be a nationwide television network, will increase its signal by 80 percent through the cable network. (Hospodarske Noviny, March 17, 1997)
BRAND-NAME PRODUCTS AND MARKETS:
-- Pepsi-Cola began selling Dr Pepper soft drink in the Czech Republic on March 5. (Strategie, March 12-19, 1997)

-- McDonalds now has over 50 restaurants in Hungary and serves an average 30 million Hungarian customers a year. Its turnover in Hungary has grown thirty-fold since 1989. (Napi Gazdasag, March 18, 1997)

-- 1996 Audi Hungaria Motor Kft in Hungary made 42.3 million ($25.1 million) German marks in profit in 1996, while turnover soared to 521.8 million marks from 291 million in 1995. Next year Audi will launch the assembly of Audi TT models in Hungary.
(Napi Gazdasag, March 19, 1997)

-- The Yugoslavian automotive company Zastava will begin selling its passenger car Yugo in the Czech Republic again and will also offer its utility vehicle Iveco Zastava. Sales should begin in May. (Pravo, March 20, 1997)

-- IBM chose the Czech Republic as a guinea-pig for its marketing project to support sales of its AS/400 computers. The project, which began in February in Prague, is aimed primarily at small- and medium-sized businesses. (Reflex, March 17, 1997)
CONSUMER TRENDS:

-- Becherovka is the most popular liqueur in the Czech Republic, according to a survey by the agency AISA. The second most favoured liqueur is egg cognac, followed by Bailey's, Fernet and Griotka. (Pravo, March 20, 1997)

-- Instant coffee consumption in western Poland is up to 250 percent greater than in eastern provinces. In urban areas around Poland instant coffee sales are several hundred percent higher than in the villages, according to a survey contracted by coffee traders. (Gazeta Wyborcza, Market research supplement March-April, 1997)
